A multilayer printed circuit board (PCB) configured for optical transmission includes at least a first layer, a second layer, and a transparent layer positioned between the first and second layers. The transparent layer provides an optical transmission region through which light can propagate within the PCB structure.

In one implementation, the transparent layer includes a first compartment. The first compartment may contain a mirror positioned to receive an incoming light beam carrying an optical signal. The mirror is configured to reflect the incoming light beam in multiple directions, including directions that are perpendicular to one another. In this way, the optical signal can be redirected and distributed within the first compartment of the transparent layer.

As the reflected light propagates through the first compartment, it carries the optical signal to different locations within the transparent layer. Additional mirrors positioned within the first compartment may receive portions of the reflected light. These mirrors can further redirect the optical signal as needed, allowing the optical signal to be routed through the PCB without relying solely on conventional electrical traces.

In some configurations, a second mirror within the first compartment is arranged to receive the reflected light carrying the optical signal and to reflect that optical signal toward an optical receiver. The optical receiver may then detect the light and convert the optical signal into an electrical signal for further processing by components associated with the multilayer PCB. This arrangement enables optical signal distribution and routing within the PCB while maintaining integration with conventional PCB layer structures.

A multilayer printed circuit board (PCB) for optical transmission includes, in addition to conventional electrical wiring layers, at least one optically transparent layer arranged between PCB layers. The transparent layer forms an internal optical path or compartment through which light can travel inside the board. One or more mirrors are positioned at selected locations in or adjacent to this transparent layer so that an incoming light beam can be redirected within the PCB.

In operation, an optical signal may enter the transparent layer from an optical transmitter, an optical fiber, a light-emitting component, or another optical coupling element. When the light beam reaches a mirror, the mirror reflects the beam into a different direction. By arranging multiple mirrors at different positions and orientations, the beam can be routed across the internal compartment in several perpendicular directions, such as horizontally along the plane of the board and vertically between layers or coupling regions. In this way, the PCB can guide optical signals through its internal structure without relying solely on external optical fibers or surface-mounted optical paths.

Additional mirrors may be provided to receive and redirect the transmitted beam toward another area of the board, toward another transparent optical channel, or toward an optical receiver. The receiver may then convert the optical signal into an electrical signal for use by electronic components mounted on or embedded within the PCB. Conversely, electrical signals generated by components on the board may be converted into optical signals and distributed through the transparent layer to other locations.

This arrangement enables board-level optical communication to be integrated directly into a multilayer PCB. Optical distribution within the board can reduce the need for long electrical interconnects, improve signal transmission at high data rates, and help minimize electromagnetic interference. The described structure therefore supports compact, high-speed communication between components, modules, or functional areas of the same printed circuit board while maintaining compatibility with multilayer PCB construction techniques.
outputs.L5:
**The PCB: A Foundation of Modern Electronics**

A **PCB**, or **printed circuit board**, is one of the most important components in modern electronic devices. It provides the physical structure and electrical connections needed for electronic components to work together. From smartphones and computers to medical devices, cars, and household appliances, almost every electronic product depends on a PCB.

The main purpose of a PCB is to connect components such as resistors, capacitors, microchips, and connectors using copper pathways called traces. These traces replace traditional wiring, making electronic circuits smaller, more reliable, and easier to manufacture. A PCB can be simple, with only one layer, or highly complex, with multiple layers designed for advanced devices.

The design of a PCB is a critical step in electronics development. Engineers must carefully plan the layout to ensure that signals move correctly, power is distributed safely, and components do not interfere with each other. Good PCB design improves performance, reduces errors, and helps extend the life of the final product.

The PCB manufacturing process involves several stages, including design, printing, etching, drilling, soldering, and testing. Each stage must be completed with precision to ensure the board functions properly. As technology continues to advance, PCBs are becoming smaller, faster, and more efficient.

In short, the PCB is the backbone of electronic technology. Without it, the compact and powerful devices we use every day would not be possible.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style description for an optical multilayer printed circuit board labeled PCB 160, including layers 1510 and 1520, transparent layer 212, compartment 1851, mirrors 214 and 1508, beam 260B/260C, and receiver 1705.
counterfactuals.output:
In some embodiments, an optical multilayer printed circuit board (“PCB”) 160 includes a plurality of stacked conductive, dielectric, and optical layers configured to support both electrical interconnection and optical signal propagation. The PCB 160 may include a first layer 1510 and a second layer 1520 disposed in a laminated stack. One or more of the layers 1510, 1520 may include electrical traces, vias, ground planes, power planes, optical alignment features, or combinations thereof.

A transparent layer 212 may be disposed within or between layers of the PCB 160. The transparent layer 212 may comprise glass, polymer, optical-grade resin, transparent dielectric material, or another material suitable for transmitting an optical beam. In one embodiment, the transparent layer 212 forms at least part of an optical path within the PCB 160 and is configured to guide, transmit, or permit passage of an optical beam through a portion of the multilayer structure.

The PCB 160 may further include a compartment 1851 formed in, through, or adjacent to one or more layers of the PCB 160. The compartment 1851 may be defined by an opening, cavity, recess, cutout, molded region, or plated or non-plated void. In certain embodiments, the compartment 1851 is configured to house, align, or expose optical components associated with an optical communication path. The compartment 1851 may extend through layer 1510, layer 1520, the transparent layer 212, or a combination thereof, depending on the desired optical routing arrangement.

A first mirror 214 may be positioned relative to the transparent layer 212 to redirect an optical beam propagating within or through the PCB 160. A second mirror 1508 may be disposed at another location in the PCB 160, for example within the compartment 1851 or adjacent to one of the layers 1510, 1520. The mirrors 214 and 1508 may comprise reflective coatings, angled reflective surfaces, metallized surfaces, dielectric mirrors, embedded prisms, micro-mirrors, or other beam-directing structures.

During operation, an optical beam 260B may propagate through the transparent layer 212 along a first optical path. The mirror 214 may receive the beam 260B and redirect it toward another region of the PCB 160. In some embodiments, the redirected beam may be transmitted as beam 260C toward the mirror 1508. The mirror 1508 may further redirect, fold, or focus the beam 260C toward an optical receiver 1705.

The receiver 1705 may be mounted on, embedded in, or optically coupled to the PCB 160. In one embodiment, the receiver 1705 is disposed in optical alignment with the compartment 1851 such that the beam 260C, after reflection by mirror 1508, is incident upon an active receiving surface of the receiver 1705. The receiver 1705 may comprise a photodiode, photodetector array, optical transceiver component, avalanche photodiode, CMOS optical sensor, or another optoelectronic device configured to convert received optical energy into an electrical signal.

In some embodiments, the layers 1510 and 1520 provide mechanical support and electrical routing for the receiver 1705 while the transparent layer 212 provides an embedded optical transmission medium. The compartment 1851 may provide an optical clearance region, an alignment region, or a mounting region for one or more optical elements. The mirrors 214 and 1508 may enable non-linear optical routing within the PCB 160, including vertical-to-horizontal, horizontal-to-vertical, or folded optical paths through the multilayer stack.

Accordingly, the PCB 160 may provide an integrated electro-optical interconnect structure in which optical beam 260B/260C is routed through the transparent layer 212 and redirected by mirrors 214 and 1508 toward receiver 1705. Such an arrangement may reduce the need for external optical fibers or free-space optical alignment structures, while allowing optical communication to be incorporated within a multilayer printed circuit board architecture.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a technical summary of an invention involving a transparent layer inside a multilayer PCB that uses mirrors to distribute an optical signal in multiple perpendicular directions.
counterfactuals.output:
The invention concerns a multilayer printed circuit board (PCB) that incorporates an internal transparent optical layer for distributing optical signals within the board. The transparent layer is embedded between conventional PCB layers and acts as an optical transmission medium, enabling light to propagate laterally through the board instead of relying solely on electrical traces.

An optical signal is introduced into the transparent layer, for example from an optical transmitter, fiber interface, or optoelectronic component mounted on or coupled to the PCB. Within the transparent layer, a set of reflective elements, such as mirrors or metallized/angled reflective surfaces, is positioned to redirect the propagating light. These mirrors are arranged so that the optical signal can be split or routed in multiple directions that are perpendicular to one another, such as along orthogonal X and Y axes within the PCB plane, and potentially toward different board locations or layers.

By using mirrors embedded in or adjacent to the transparent layer, the system can distribute a single optical signal to multiple destinations across the PCB without requiring separate point-to-point optical paths for each receiver. The reflective structures may be formed at selected angles, such as approximately 45 degrees, to redirect light by about 90 degrees, allowing controlled optical routing around the board. Multiple mirrors may be placed at different positions to create a network of optical distribution paths.

The multilayer PCB may also include conventional conductive layers, dielectric layers, vias, and electronic components. Optoelectronic receivers or coupling structures can be located at predetermined positions to extract the optical signal from the transparent layer and convert it into electrical signals. This enables high-speed, low-loss signal distribution while reducing electromagnetic interference compared with purely electrical interconnects.

In summary, the invention provides an optical interconnect architecture integrated inside a multilayer PCB. A transparent internal layer functions as a light guide, while embedded mirrors distribute an incoming optical signal in multiple perpendicular directions to serve different components or regions of the board. This approach supports compact optical signal routing, improved bandwidth, reduced electrical noise, and simplified distribution of high-speed signals in complex electronic assemblies.

## Patent Specification Excerpt

### Title  
**Optical Signal Transmission Through a Compartment in a Transparent Layer of a Multilayer Printed Circuit Board Using Embedded Mirrors**

### Technical Field  
The present disclosure relates generally to multilayer printed circuit boards and, more particularly, to optical signal transmission structures integrated within multilayer printed circuit boards using transparent dielectric layers, optical compartments, and embedded reflective elements configured to direct light beams between optical emitters and optical receivers.

### Background  
As data rates in electronic systems increase, conventional conductive signal traces in printed circuit boards may experience losses, crosstalk, electromagnetic interference, and bandwidth limitations. Optical interconnects provide an alternative signal transmission path capable of supporting high-speed communication with reduced electromagnetic coupling. However, incorporating optical paths into multilayer printed circuit boards presents challenges, including alignment of optical components, routing of optical beams through board layers, and integration with conventional manufacturing processes.

Accordingly, there is a need for an integrated optical transmission arrangement within a multilayer printed circuit board that enables controlled propagation of optical signals through a transparent layer while allowing redirection of the optical beam between layers or between laterally spaced components.

### Summary  
In one embodiment, a multilayer printed circuit board includes a plurality of conductive layers and dielectric layers, at least one of the dielectric layers comprising an optically transparent material. A compartment is formed in or adjacent to the optically transparent layer and defines an optical propagation region. A first optical device, such as a laser diode, light-emitting diode, or optical transmitter, is arranged to emit an optical signal into the compartment. One or more embedded mirrors are positioned within or along boundaries of the compartment to reflect the emitted optical signal along a predetermined optical path through the transparent layer. A second optical device, such as a photodiode or optical receiver, is arranged to receive the reflected optical signal.

In certain embodiments, the embedded mirrors comprise metallized surfaces, dielectric reflective coatings, total internal reflection interfaces, angled mirror inserts, or reflective sidewalls formed during fabrication of the multilayer printed circuit board. The mirrors may be disposed at approximately forty-five degrees relative to a principal plane of the board to redirect light between a direction normal to the board and a direction substantially parallel to the board plane. Multiple mirrors may be used to route the light beam around conductive structures, vias, components, or opaque dielectric regions within the board.

### Detailed Description  

Referring generally to an exemplary multilayer printed circuit board, the board may include a stack of alternating conductive and dielectric layers laminated together to form a unitary structure. At least one dielectric layer of the stack is formed from an optically transparent polymer, glass-reinforced transparent resin, optical-grade epoxy, polyimide, acrylic material, or other material having sufficient transmissivity at a selected wavelength of operation. The selected wavelength may be, by way of example, in the visible, near-infrared, or infrared range.

A compartment is provided within the transparent layer. The compartment may be formed as a cavity, channel, recess, void, filled optical guide region, or locally defined region having optical properties different from adjacent board material. In one implementation, the compartment comprises an air-filled or gas-filled cavity bounded at least in part by surfaces of the transparent dielectric layer. In another implementation, the compartment is filled with a transparent optical medium, such as a cured resin, index-matching gel, or molded optical material.

An optical transmitter is optically coupled to the compartment. The optical transmitter may be mounted on an exterior surface of the printed circuit board, embedded within a cavity of the board, or mounted on an internal substrate layer prior to lamination. The transmitter is configured to emit a light beam into the compartment. The light beam may enter the transparent layer through an aperture, window, lens, coupling surface, or optically transmissive via.

A first embedded mirror is positioned to intercept the light beam emitted by the transmitter. The first embedded mirror may be formed on an inclined surface of the compartment, such as a beveled or sloped wall. The inclined surface may be coated with a reflective material including, but not limited to, aluminum, silver, gold, copper, nickel, or a multilayer dielectric reflector. In some embodiments, the reflective surface is produced by laser ablation, mechanical drilling, micromachining, molding, stamping, photolithographic patterning, or controlled removal of dielectric material followed by metallization.

The first embedded mirror reflects the light beam into a propagation direction within the transparent layer. In an exemplary configuration, the transmitter emits light in a direction generally perpendicular to a major surface of the printed circuit board, and the first embedded mirror redirects the light beam into a direction generally parallel to the major surface. The reflected light beam then travels through the compartment or through the transparent dielectric material toward a second embedded mirror.

The second embedded mirror may be spaced laterally from the first embedded mirror and oriented to redirect the light beam toward an optical receiver. For example, the second embedded mirror may reflect the light beam from a path substantially parallel to the board surface to a path substantially perpendicular to the board surface. The optical receiver is positioned to receive the redirected beam and convert the optical signal into an electrical signal. In some embodiments, the receiver is mounted on the same side of the printed circuit board as the transmitter; in other embodiments, the receiver is mounted on an opposite side or is embedded within the board.

The compartment may provide a controlled optical path isolated from surrounding conductive traces, solder masks, opaque dielectric materials, vias, and electronic components. The compartment may be dimensioned to reduce beam clipping and scattering and may include beam-shaping structures such as lenses, collimators, apertures, waveguide transitions, or index-gradient regions. The transparent layer may further include alignment features configured to maintain positional accuracy between the embedded mirrors and the optical devices.

In certain embodiments, the embedded mirrors are arranged to produce multiple reflections, thereby routing the optical signal along a non-linear path. Such a configuration may allow optical communication between devices positioned at different locations on the printed circuit board while avoiding physical obstacles. The mirrors may also divide or combine optical beams, for example by using partially reflective coatings, wavelength-selective coatings, or beam-splitting surfaces.

The optical signal transmission structure may be fabricated as part of a multilayer printed circuit board manufacturing process. A transparent dielectric sheet may be patterned to form the compartment and angled mirror surfaces. Reflective coatings may then be deposited on selected surfaces. The transparent dielectric sheet may be laminated with other dielectric and conductive layers. Openings may be provided through one or more layers to permit optical coupling between surface-mounted or embedded optical components and the compartment.

The disclosed arrangement enables optical transmission within a multilayer printed circuit board without requiring a separate optical fiber routed on the board surface. By embedding the reflective elements and using a transparent layer as an optical propagation medium, high-speed optical interconnects may be integrated with conventional electrical interconnects in a compact structure.

### Exemplary Embodiments  

In one exemplary embodiment, a multilayer printed circuit board comprises a transparent dielectric layer disposed between first and second conductive layers. A compartment extends laterally within the transparent dielectric layer. A first mirror is formed at a first end of the compartment and is inclined at approximately forty-five degrees relative to the transparent dielectric layer. A second mirror is formed at a second end of the compartment and is similarly inclined. A light-emitting device mounted on a surface of the board emits a modulated light beam through an opening toward the first mirror. The first mirror reflects the light beam laterally through the compartment. The second mirror reflects the light beam toward a photodetector mounted at another location on the board.

In another exemplary embodiment, the compartment is filled with a transparent material having a refractive index selected to confine or guide the optical beam. The mirrors comprise dielectric multilayer coatings optimized for a wavelength emitted by a vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser. The optical receiver comprises a photodiode aligned with an output aperture formed through one or more layers of the printed circuit board.

In yet another exemplary embodiment, a plurality of optical channels are formed in a common transparent layer, each optical channel having associated embedded mirrors for routing separate optical signals. The optical channels may be arranged in parallel to provide a multi-channel optical bus within the multilayer printed circuit board.

### Representative Claim-Style Language  

1. A multilayer printed circuit board comprising:  
   a stack including a plurality of conductive layers and a plurality of dielectric layers;  
   a transparent layer disposed within the stack;  
   a compartment formed in the transparent layer and defining an optical propagation path;  
   a first optical device configured to emit a light beam into the compartment;  
   a first embedded mirror positioned to reflect the light beam along the optical propagation path through the transparent layer;  
   a second embedded mirror positioned to redirect the reflected light beam; and  
   a second optical device positioned to receive the redirected light beam.

2. The multilayer printed circuit board of claim 1, wherein at least one of the first embedded mirror and the second embedded mirror comprises an inclined reflective surface coated with a metallic reflective coating.

3. The multilayer printed circuit board of claim 1, wherein the first embedded mirror is configured to redirect the light beam from a direction substantially perpendicular to a major surface of the printed circuit board to a direction substantially parallel to the major surface.

4. The multilayer printed circuit board of claim 1, wherein the compartment comprises an air-filled cavity within the transparent layer.

5. The multilayer printed circuit board of claim 1, wherein the compartment comprises a transparent optical medium having a refractive index selected to guide the light beam between the first embedded mirror and the second embedded mirror.
